5350bf28e1d5ddd91dff679e903ed51888b06f5b.answer:
Each driver is allocated **8 sets of soft-specification dry-weather tyres** at a Standard Format Competition [1].

The table in [1] is poorly formatted, so this reading depends on matching the column order. The first column of values corresponds to the Standard Format Competition, and the soft-tyre row gives 8 there. Under the Standard Format Competition with ICTT, the allocation is 6 soft sets [1].

9815509996938149e294069c340e1b8320fd105f.answer:
Generally, no. Work on a car in the Fast Lane is prohibited unless a specific exception applies. Competitors may not work on a car or leave equipment in the Fast Lane, except as detailed in Articles B5.3.3 and B5.14.4a [3]. The Inner Lane is otherwise the only area where work on an F1 car can be carried out [2][3].

The exception in Article B5.3.3 covers cars starting from the end of the Pit Lane. Work there is permitted until 15 seconds before the formation lap begins, after which all personnel and equipment must be clear of the Fast Lane [1]. Permitted work is limited to:

- Starting the engine and directly associated preparation.
- Fitting or removing permitted cooling and heating devices.
- Changes made for driver comfort.
- Changing wheels and tyres, subject to Article B5.5.3.
- Adjusting the front wing profiles, where not controlled by the FIA Standard ECU, under Article C3.10.10. No parts may be added, removed, or replaced [1].

Drivers must follow marshals' directions at all times [1]. Even where work is otherwise allowed, it may not be carried out in the Fast Lane if it is likely to hinder other F1 cars attempting to leave the Pit Lane [2][3].

The passages do not cover Article B5.14.4a, which is the other exception cited, so they do not say what work it permits.

a8d90cb842c0e440ffd1d49f12dfc0541f6d2715.answer:
Under the passages provided, a team can replace parts on a car in parc fermé only in two situations:

1. **Work listed in Appendix B2.** Article B3.5.3 bars replacing or modifying any part of the car, except for work listed in Appendix B2 or approved by the Technical Delegate under Article B3.5.4 [1]. Appendix B2 itself is not included in the passages.

2. **Work approved by the Technical Delegate.** The same article allows work that the Technical Delegate approves under Article B3.5.4 [1]. Article B3.5.9 adds that parts replaced with the Technical Delegate's specific agreement while cars are under parc fermé conditions must be published and distributed to all Competitors before the Race [2].

Any replacement outside these exceptions breaches parc fermé. The penalty depends on the format: at a Standard Format Competition, the driver must start the Race from the Pit Lane. At an Alternative Format Competition, a breach before the Sprint start means starting the Sprint from the Pit Lane, and a breach after Qualifying has started means starting the Race from the Pit Lane [1].

The passages do not contain the text of Article B3.5.4 or Appendix B2, so they do not say which specific parts are permitted or how the Technical Delegate grants approval. Article B3.5.7 also limits changes to suspension and aerodynamic configuration, except the front wing, to those that clearly require tools, but it does not give permission for any change [3].

1e8cbf4978ec44429349613622b6531cb891f2db.answer:
A team may replace or modify parts on a car in parc fermé only in two situations:

1. **Work listed in Appendix B2.** Article B3.5.3 says that, apart from the sealing provided for in Articles B3.4.2 and B3.4.3, only work listed in Appendix B2 may be carried out [1]. Appendix B2 permits:
   - Adjusting tyre pressures [3].
   - Weighing the car using an allocated tyre set or travel tyres [3].
   - Fitting exhaust extraction devices while starting the engine in the garage [3].
   - Changing the survival cell, but only if the car has suffered genuine accident damage or a significant failure or fault. All components of the replacement car must match the original in design and be similar in mass, inertia and function, and the suspension set-up must be the same [3].

2. **Work approved by the Technical Delegate.** Work approved by the Technical Delegate under Article B3.5.4 is also allowed [1]. Appendix B2 also covers any other work the Technical Delegate requests [3]. The excerpts do not include the text of Article B3.5.4, so they do not say how that approval is obtained.

Outside these cases, no part may be replaced or modified, and no changes may be made to the car's setup or configuration [1].

If parc fermé conditions are breached, the consequences depend on the format. At a Standard Format Competition, the driver must start the Race from the Pit Lane. At an Alternative Format Competition, a breach before the Sprint means the Sprint starts from the Pit Lane, and a breach after Qualifying has started means the Race starts from the Pit Lane [1].

7e2c276870883b7554392a9b0929aae36ec89f5e.answer:
For an incident during a TTCS, the stewards may impose any one of these penalties on any driver involved [2]:

- a. A 5-second time penalty
- b. A 10-second time penalty
- c. A drive-through penalty
- d. A 10-second stop-and-go penalty
- e. A time penalty
- f. A driver reprimand
- g. A Competitor (F1 Team) reprimand

Stewards must also not penalise a driver unless it is clear that the driver was wholly or predominantly to blame [1]. They may impose these penalties in addition to or instead of other penalties available under the ISC [1].

Separately, a driver who receives five reprimands (at least four for driving infringements) in the same Championship receives a 10-grid-place penalty. If the fifth reprimand follows an incident during a Race, the grid penalty applies at the driver's next Competition [2].

The passages do not define "TTCS" or explicitly state that a Race is a TTCS. The answer above assumes the Race falls under that heading, since the reprimand rule refers to incidents "during a Race" as a separate case.

2c57dd5d1555b4b0e8937bcefa76a9fa2db7a4ac.answer:
The passages do not directly list the penalties for an incident during the Race. They give related rules, though.

- **Penalties for incidents during a TTCS [1]:** The stewards may impose any one of these on any driver involved: a 5-second penalty, a 10-second penalty, a drive-through penalty, a 10-second stop-and-go penalty, a time penalty, a driver reprimand, or a Competitor (F1 Team) reprimand. The passages do not state whether a Race falls under the TTCS rules.

- **Penalties for incidents during an LTCS [2]:** The stewards may delete a driver's lap time(s) or drop the driver a number of grid positions. Any grid position penalty is served in the Race, unless the infringement occurred in Sprint Qualifying, in which case it applies to the Sprint grid.

- **General discretion [3]:** The stewards decide whether a driver involved in an Incident should be penalised. No penalty is imposed unless the stewards judge the driver wholly or predominantly to blame. The stewards may impose the penalties specified in the regulations in addition to or instead of other penalties available under the ISC.

- **Race-specific reference [1]:** A driver who receives five reprimands (at least four for driving infringements) in the same Championship receives a ten-grid-place penalty. If the fifth reprimand follows an incident during a Race, the penalty is applied at the driver's next Competition.

68eede8db92ce70ff4e3c9d70773d058e5954a41.answer:
Cars may only pass each other behind the Safety Car when the Race Director instructs it. The green light on the Safety Car is illuminated to tell F1 Cars between it and the leader that they must pass. Those cars then continue at reduced speed, without overtaking, until they reach the queue behind the Safety Car [3a].

The restriction ends once all those cars have passed the Safety Car. At that point the green light is extinguished, which signals that overtaking is no longer permitted [3a][1]. The exception is the cases listed in Article B5.13.2c, but those are not included in the passages provided.

Lapped cars follow a separate procedure:
- The Race Director may allow them to overtake if it is considered safe. The message "LAPPED CARS MAY NOW OVERTAKE" is sent, and the Safety Car's green light is illuminated for lapped cars to pass the cars on the lead lap and the Safety Car [3c].
- This applies only to cars that were lapped when they crossed the Control Line at the end of the lap in which they crossed the first safety car line for the second time after deployment [3c].
- If the Race Director considers track conditions unsuitable, "OVERTAKING WILL NOT BE PERMITTED" is sent instead [3b].
- Cars on the lead lap must stay on the racing line while lapped cars overtake them, unless deviating is unavoidable [3c][1].
- Once past, the cars proceed without overtaking and take up position at the back of the queue behind the Safety Car [1].

Finally, the Safety Car stays deployed at least until the leader is behind it and all remaining F1 Cars are queued behind it [2a]. After "LAPPED CARS MAY NOW OVERTAKE" is sent, it returns to the pits at the end of the following lap unless the Race Director considers it still necessary [2b].

c1704b639b8de3d0155abea87bbf21299f6f1ecc.answer:
Behind the Safety Car, overtaking is allowed only when the Race Director signals it, and the restriction returns once the cars that need to pass have done so.

**Cars between the Safety Car and the leader:** When the Race Director instructs, the Safety Car's green light is illuminated to tell the F1 Cars between it and the leader that they must pass. Once all such cars have passed, the green light is extinguished, and overtaking is no longer permitted. These cars then continue at reduced speed without overtaking until they reach the queue behind the Safety Car [2].

**Lapped cars:** If the Race Director considers it safe, "LAPPED CARS MAY NOW OVERTAKE" is sent to all competitors, and the green light tells lapped cars to pass the lead-lap cars and the Safety Car. This applies only to cars that were lapped when they crossed the Control Line at the end of the lap on which they first crossed the first safety car line for the second time after the Safety Car was deployed [2]. While this happens, lead-lap cars must stay on the racing line unless deviating from it is unavoidable [2][3].

**When the restriction ends:** Once all such cars have passed the Safety Car, the green light is extinguished and overtaking is no longer permitted, except in the cases listed in Article B5.13.2c [2][3]. Cars that have been overtaken should then proceed at an appropriate speed, without overtaking, and make every effort to rejoin the back of the queue behind the Safety Car [3]. The Race Director may also close the Pit Lane exit while cars are rejoining the queue [3].

**Formation lap:** Separately, overtaking during the formation lap behind the Safety Car is permitted only in limited cases, such as when a car is delayed leaving the grid or slows with an obvious problem. In those cases, drivers may overtake only to re-establish the original starting order or the order at the Pit Lane exit when the formation lap started [1].

The passages do not define Article B5.13.2c, so the exceptions to the end of the restriction cannot be specified from them.

2eac2fdcecf1ca64d689b5c7ed1db4bbe6c45eb5.answer:
The passages don't address a start that is halted, but they cover the two procedures that follow the formation laps, standing start and rolling start.

**Standing start:** Once the "STANDING START" message is sent, the Pit Lane exit closes and the Safety Car's orange lights go out. Once the Safety Car has entered the Pit Lane, all F1 Cars, except those required to start from the Pit Lane, can return to the grid and take their grid positions [2]. Cars required to start from the Pit Lane must re-enter the Pit Lane and may start once the Pit Lane exit opens after the start [2].

**Rolling start:** After the "ROLLING START" message, the Pit Lane exit closes and the orange lights go out. Drivers must keep a steady pace with no erratic acceleration or braking, and no car may be driven alongside a car ahead, until the Safety Car enters the Pit Entry Road [3]. No driver may overtake another F1 Car until passing the Control Line for the first time after the Safety Car has entered the Pit Entry Road [3].

**Order:** Any overtaking to fix a delayed car's position is only allowed to restore the original starting order or the order at the Pit Lane exit when the formation lap started [1]. In a standing start, a delayed driver may overtake to regain the original starting position only before crossing the first safety car line on the lap the Safety Car returns to the pits. Otherwise, the driver must re-enter the Pit Lane and may rejoin only after the whole field has passed the end of the Pit Lane following the start of the TTCS [1].

f574a39adce25e74469e0e2ad309c3323c813c9d.answer:
If the starting procedure is suspended after the formation laps behind the Safety Car have begun, all F1 Cars must enter the Pit Lane behind the Safety Car [1].

- **Where they go:** The first F1 Car to enter the Pit Lane goes directly to the Pit Lane exit, unless the Race Director has defined another location in the Pit Lane [1].
- **Order:** All other F1 Cars form up in a line behind the first car, in the order they entered the Pit Lane behind the Safety Car when the procedure was suspended [1].
- **Lane:** All cars must stay in the Fast Lane [1].

In exceptional circumstances, for safety reasons, the pit entry may be closed before the F1 Cars have returned to the Pit Lane. In that case, all F1 Cars must proceed slowly to the starting grid. The first car to arrive on the grid takes pole position, and the others fill the remaining grid positions in the order they arrive [1].

After this, the procedures in Article B5.15 must be followed [1].

126d69154160cee5e0f6c649d51c0ecac8f9f70a.answer:
The passages don't mention Q1 or Q2 by name, so they don't directly describe how knockout-stage results are handled. They do explain how the race grid is built from Qualifying classification, which is the basis for the placings.

- **Starting point:** The race grid is formed from Qualifying results and the Qualifying classification process (Article B2.4.3) [2].
- **Penalised classified drivers:** Drivers with 15 or fewer cumulative grid penalties get a temporary position equal to their Qualifying classification plus their penalty places [2].
- **Unpenalised classified drivers:** They fill any unoccupied grid position in Qualifying classification order [2][1].
- **Penalised drivers moved up:** Penalised drivers with a temporary position are then moved up to fill any remaining gaps [1].
- **Drivers with more than 15 penalties:** They start behind all other classified drivers, ordered by Qualifying classification [1].
- **Unclassified drivers:** Drivers the Stewards have allowed to take part start behind all classified drivers, in an order set by Article B2.4.3b, which is not included in the passages [1].

A driver knocked out in Q1 or Q2 is still classified in Qualifying, so their race grid position follows from that classification using the steps above. The exact rules for how Q1 and Q2 eliminations translate into classification are in Article B2.4.3, which is not included here.

0ce6aa2df4b98e5427c30e9e346f35aacce2facb.answer:
Drivers eliminated in Q1 and Q2 are placed by their fastest lap time in the session they were knocked out of, with the later session's drivers ahead:

- **Q2 eliminations:** The next six positions, 11th through 16th, go to drivers eliminated in Q2, ordered by their fastest Q2 lap time, with the fastest in 11th [2].
- **Q1 eliminations:** The next six positions, 17th through 22nd, go to drivers eliminated in Q1, ordered by their fastest Q1 lap time, with the fastest in 17th [2].

If drivers set identical times in a session, the driver who set that time first is ranked higher [2]. If more than one driver fails to set a lap time in Q2 or Q3, they are ordered by whether they attempted a flying lap, then whether they started one, then whether they left the pits. Within each group, the previous session's classification decides [2].

These positions assume 22 eligible cars. With 20 cars, five drivers are eliminated after Q1 and Q2 instead, and with 24 cars, seven are eliminated [3].

The passages describe this as the Qualifying Classification, and they do not explicitly say it sets the race grid. They also do not cover how drivers whose lap times are disallowed or who are disqualified are placed, beyond the separate "unclassified" rules in [1].

277bc044138676e45bb3717b0f42032beb4f76cd.answer:
The provided passages don't directly answer this. They cover component age only for tests that happen after the season, not before the first race.

The pre-season tests (the Private Collective Testing in B11.2.7a and the Public Collective Testing in B11.2.7b) are described in [3], but those passages set out only the number of tests, days, and cars per day. They say nothing about which components or software may be used.

The rules on older components that do appear apply to the Post-Season Test, which takes place after the last Competition of the Championship [1]. For that test, one car must use only components and software that were used in at least one Race or TCC in the current year or the preceding year [1]. Tyre-test changes are also restricted: replacement components should match the original specification, and a different specification may be approved only if the same one is unavailable and it was previously used at a Competition or TCC [2].

The passages also restrict parts for TPC (Article B11.3), which is a separate testing category rather than the pre-season tests. Under that rule, no parts or changes may give information related to current-Championship cars, and only instrumentation fitted at one or more Races of the period is permitted [2].

c05f0cc032ff4b1e262945577743b810df971dd6.answer:
The passages don't directly answer this. They don't set out what older parts may be used before the first race of the season.

The closest rules concern testing after the first Competition. For tests between the end of the first Competition and 31 December, teams must use a "Mule Car" meeting one of two conditions:

- **Option i:** A car built to the current Championship's technical regulations, using only components and software that were used in at least one Race or TCC during the current year or the four years before it [1].
- **Option ii:** A car built to the technical regulations of any of the four preceding calendar years, using only components and software that were used in at least one Race or TCC during those four years [1].

Passage 1 refers to Article B11.4.10b, which is not included, so I can't rule out whether it covers the pre-season period.

For the Post-Season Test, which takes place after the last Competition, one F1 Car must use only components and software used in a Race or TCC during the current year or the preceding year [2]. This applies to a different test, so it doesn't answer the pre-season question.

2c5a5ed9076e844e543e308033a04ec806c383de.answer:
The passages don't use the term "tyre checks," so I'm assuming you mean tyre-related running. Under that reading, the relevant provisions are these:

**Post-Season Test (tyre specification testing)**
- **When:** One test, one day long, commencing no less than 36 hours after the end of the last Competition of the Championship [2].
- **Where:** On the circuit where the last Competition of the Championship was held [2].
- **Car:** One F1 Car is used for the sole purpose of letting Competitors test the tyre specifications for the following season. It must use components and software that were used in at least one Race or TCC in the current year or the preceding year. This does not apply to Power Units or their associated software [2].
- **Sensors:** Additional sensors may be fitted only to measure tyre state or performance. They must be agreed in advance with the Tyre Supplier and the FIA, and the data must be shared with the Tyre Supplier after the session [3].

**Wet-weather tyre testing**
- One day may be set aside if the Tyre Supplier requests it. Arrangements are made in consultation with all Competitors, the Commercial Rights Holder and the FIA [2]. The passages give no specific time or location limits for this day.

**Out-of-Competition Tyre Testing**
- Article B11.2.7d is referenced for tyre-specification running [3], but its text is not in the provided passages, so I can't state its time or location limits.

f659fc19c2d0aa6aa889f7a48637f289f7d9ad5b.answer:
The passages only partly answer this. They do not give the time or location limits for tyre testing.

**What is covered:**

- **Permitted cars:** For Out-of-Competition Tyre Testing (Article B11.2.7d), a Current Car, a Previous Car, or a Mule Car may be on the track. All other car types are excluded [2].
- **Set-up changes:** Mechanical set-up changes and driver control changes are allowed only if they are necessary for the correct evaluation of the tyres or to complete the tyre test. They must be agreed in advance with the tyre supplier [3].

**What is not covered:**

- The passages do not state when tyre testing may take place (for example, a date range or a period relative to the Championship or Competitions).
- They do not state any location restrictions, such as which circuits are allowed.

The rules on testing timing and location in [1] (Article B11.4.10) apply to TMC testing, not tyre testing. Article B11.2.7d, which sets out the tyre-testing provisions in full, is not included in the passages, so the time and location limits would need to be checked there.
